necessary_same_A_page_experiment.statement:
## Setup

The experiment used $^7\mathrm{Li}^+$ ions from a Penning ion gauge source, accelerated to $58.6\,\mathrm{MeV/u}$ and stored in the ESR at nominal $\beta=0.338$. Electron cooling reduced the reported longitudinal velocity spread to $\delta v/v\approx9\times10^{-6}$ (FWHM) and transverse divergence to less than $100\,\mu\mathrm{rad}$. About $10^7$ to $10^8$ ions were stored, with an estimated metastable fraction below $1\%$. The metastable $3S_1$ lifetime was $15$–$30\,\mathrm{s}$ in the ring, compared with $50\,\mathrm{s}$ in vacuum. The Lambda system used the transitions $3S_1(F=3/2)\to3P_2(F=5/2)$ and $3S_1(F=5/2)\to3P_2(F=5/2)$. Parallel and antiparallel beams near $386\,\mathrm{nm}$ and $780\,\mathrm{nm}$ addressed its two legs; an additional $780\,\mathrm{nm}$ beam repumped ions into the system.

## Procedure

The parallel beam was generated by doubling a $772\,\mathrm{nm}$ Ti:Sa laser locked to an iodine marker previously calibrated with a frequency comb against a rubidium clock. The antiparallel diode laser was offset-locked to a rubidium reference, with a $600\,\mathrm{MHz}$ tuning range. Polarization-maintaining fibers transported the beams. Motorized stages controlled angles and positions to $20\,\mu\mathrm{rad}$ and $50\,\mu\mathrm{m}$; scrapers established laser/ion overlap within $80\,\mu\mathrm{rad}$. Photomultipliers counted fluorescence in four successive $100\,\mu\mathrm{s}$ configurations: both excitation beams, antiparallel only, parallel only, and neither. Dark counts were subtracted, then the separate-beam background was subtracted from the both-beam spectrum. Optical-optical double resonance selected ions for which both Lambda legs were resonant at the same velocity. To compensate metastable depletion, an $81$-point scan was paused after $69$ points for injection and cooling. Figure 2 shows an example averaged over $44$ scans, with $49\,\mathrm{MHz}$ laboratory linewidth and $35\,\mathrm{MHz}$ rest-frame linewidth. The authors fitted $40$ spectra with Lorentzians on linear backgrounds and formed a weighted average. Raw count tables, fit weights, a covariance matrix and a complete likelihood are not published in this report.

## Observations

Table I gives the frequency estimates, in MHz, $\nu_1=546455143.0$, $\nu_2=546474960.7$, $\nu_a=384225534.98$ and $\nu_p=777210326.98$. The rest-frame inputs $\nu_1,\nu_2$ come from earlier measurements cited as references 21–22; those papers were not retrieved or read here. Equation (4) reports $\epsilon=\sqrt{\nu_a\nu_p/(\nu_1\nu_2)}-1=(1.5\pm2.3)\times10^{-9}$ at nominal $\beta=0.338$. These are estimates with the source-labelled $1\sigma$ uncertainty budget, not exact values or guaranteed bounds. The rounded Table I centers yield approximately $1.4744849565\times10^{-9}$, consistent with the reported rounded estimate, without reconstructing unrounded data.

## Uncertainty

Table I labels its uncertainties $1\sigma$. In MHz, the aggregate entries are $0.43$ for each rest frequency, $1.6$ for the antiparallel frequency and $1.25$ for the parallel frequency. Antiparallel contributions are: weighted-fit statistical uncertainty $0.6$, rubidium reference $0.05$, diode stabilization $0.64$, background linearization $0.5$, Gouy phase $1.0$, angular alignment $0.6$, and ion divergence $0.4$. Parallel contributions are: iodine reference $0.06$, Ti:Sa stabilization $0.12$, Gouy phase $1.0$, alignment $0.6$, and divergence $0.4$. The inferred Gouy correction for each laser was $0.44\pm1.0\,\mathrm{MHz}$, from experimentally validated numerical simulation using measured beam parameters. The authors reported no significant residual asymmetry; simulated background linearization was assigned $0.5\,\mathrm{MHz}$. The excess linewidth, about five times the expected width, was attributed mainly to drift-induced fluorescence. The $0.6\,\mathrm{MHz}$ statistical entry comes from the weighted analysis of forty fitted spectra, not forty independent raw clock readings. These reported statistical and systematic scales are preserved without inventing independence, a Gaussian total sampling law, fit weights, covariance or coverage.

## Interpretation

The measured observable tests the combined Doppler/time-dilation, active atomic-transition and vacuum-wave invariance assumptions together with resonance selection, calibration, beam alignment and correction models. The source reports no resolved deviation at its uncertainty level and quotes $|\alpha|\le2.0\times10^{-8}$ for $\alpha=\epsilon/\beta^2$. That quotation is recorded as the source's test-theory sensitivity statement, rather than a newly certified hard bound or confidence interval. RMS and SME parameter translations and future higher-boost prospects remain contextual research topics; they are not prerequisites or claims of the comparison theorem.

full_statement_strategy_actually_read.title: Doppler shift and aberration for an ideal plane wave between inertial descriptions
full_statement_strategy_actually_read.statement: Adopt post-sr-inertial-covariance, post-sr-ideal-clocks-and-light and post-sr-ideal-plane-wave-model, and the conventions of def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions. Let x and x' be inertial charts whose transition is x' = B(beta) x + b with beta in R^3, |beta| < 1, b in R^4 and B(beta) the passive boost of def-lorentz-boost; write gamma := (1 - |beta|^2)^(-1/2) and beta_hat := beta/|beta| for beta nonzero, so that the frame x' moves with velocity v = c beta relative to the frame x in the direction beta_hat. Let the ideal wave of the model have phase theta with future null wave covector k and frame-x data (omega,s) in the sense of def-sr-null-wave-covector-and-observer-frequency: omega > 0, s in R^3 with |s| = 1 and k_a = (-omega/c, (omega/c)s) in x. Then, conditionally on the adopted model: (i) Frame data in x'. The data of the same covector k in x' is (omega',s') with omega' = gamma(1 - beta . s) omega > 0 and s' = [s + ((gamma - 1)/|beta|^2)(beta . s) beta - gamma beta]/[gamma(1 - beta . s)] for beta nonzero (and omega' = omega, s' = s for beta = 0), so |s'| = 1 and k'_a = (-omega'/c, (omega'/c)s'_1, (omega'/c)s'_2, (omega'/c)s'_3) in x'. In the axis case beta = b e_1 with b in (-1,1): s'_1 = (s_1 - b)/(1 - b s_1) and (s'_2,s'_3) = (s_2,s_3)/(gamma(1 - b s_1)). (ii) Reading and frequency ratios. The rest observers of x and x' (four-velocities c e_0 and c e'_0) read angular frequencies omega = -c k(e_0) and omega' = -c k(e'_0); the linear frequencies and wavelengths of the two descriptions satisfy nu' = gamma(1 - beta . s) nu and lambda' = lambda/[gamma(1 - beta . s)]. More generally, an ideal observer whose coordinate velocity in x is w (a vector of the frame's spatial three-space with |w| < c) reads omega_o = gamma_w(1 - (w . s)/c) omega, where gamma_w := (1 - |w|^2/c^2)^(-1/2); equivalently omega_o = gamma_w(1 - beta_w . s) omega with beta_w := w/c. (iii) Longitudinal cases. If s = beta_hat then omega' = omega sqrt((1 - |beta|)/(1 + |beta|)) < omega, nu' = nu sqrt((1 - |beta|)/(1 + |beta|)) and lambda' = lambda sqrt((1 + |beta|)/(1 - |beta|)): the observer moving in the direction of propagation (away from a source at rest in x and located behind it) reads a red-shifted frequency and lengthened wavelength. If s = -beta_hat then omega' = omega sqrt((1 + |beta|)/(1 - |beta|)) > omega and lambda' = lambda sqrt((1 - |beta|)/(1 + |beta|)): blue shift for an observer moving opposite to the propagation direction (toward such a source). (iv) Transverse protocols. If beta . s = 0 (propagation direction perpendicular to the relative velocity in the frame x) then omega' = gamma omega > omega. If beta . s = |beta|^2, equivalently s' . beta_hat = 0 (propagation direction perpendicular to the relative velocity in the frame x'), then omega' = omega/gamma < omega. Both configurations are called transverse Doppler configurations in the literature and the two factors differ; the direction and size of the shift are not determined by the word 'transverse' without specifying the frame in which transversality holds. (v) Aberration. If theta_x, theta_x' in [0,pi] are the angles between the propagation directions s, s' and the boost axis beta_hat, then cos theta_x' = (cos theta_x - |beta|)/(1 - |beta| cos theta_x); the map u |-> (u - |beta|)/(1 - |beta| u) is a strictly increasing bijection of [-1,1] onto itself, and in particular cos theta_x = 0 gives cos theta_x' = -|beta|. (vi) Scope and protocol. All clauses concern one ideal plane wave and ideal observers, and frequencies are compared through the phase model at specified reception events; the results are conditional on the adopted postulates (ideal plane wave, ideal clocks, inertial covariance, flat classical spacetime) and are not empirical claims about nature, sources or apparatus. They exclude media and dispersion, modulation and signal speeds, intensity and polarization, real line widths, accelerating observers (reserved to the framework's accelerated-observer page), gravitation and quantum effects; no statistical or measurement statement is made. If beta = 0 the two charts agree and omega' = omega, s' = s.
full_statement_strategy_actually_read.strategy: Proof in dependency order; the mathematical core is lem-sr-null-covector-boost-transformation with the reading lemmas. (i) By def-sr-null-wave-covector-and-observer-frequency the frame data of k in x is (omega,s) with omega = c varpi, varpi = -k(e_0), and k_a = (-omega/c,(omega/c)s). Apply lem-sr-null-covector-boost-transformation(i)-(ii) with (varpi,s): its conclusions give varpi' = gamma(1 - beta . s) varpi > 0 and the displayed s' with |s'| = 1; multiplying by c gives omega' = gamma(1 - beta . s) omega; the axis formulas are clause (iii) of the lemma. The relation beta . s = |beta|^2 <=> s' . beta_hat = 0 is clause (iv) of the lemma, and the identity s' . beta_hat = (beta . s - |beta|^2)/(|beta|(1 - beta . s)) for beta nonzero is its display. (ii) For the rest observer of x, U = c e_0 and omega = -c k(e_0) by the definition; for x' likewise with the frame vector e'_0 (def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart). The wavelength ratio is the reciprocal of the frequency ratio because lambda = c/nu and lambda' = c/nu' by definition. For a general observer write U_o = gamma_w(c,w) by thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition(e); then k(U_o) = c gamma_w k(e_0) + gamma_w k(w), and k(w) = (omega/c) w . s because w lies in the frame's spatial three-space and k_a = (-omega/c,(omega/c)s) (def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame); hence omega_o = -k(U_o) = gamma_w(omega - (omega/c) w . s) = gamma_w(1 - (w . s)/c) omega. (iii) Substitute s = +/- beta_hat into (i): gamma(1 -/+ |beta|) = sqrt((1 -/+ |beta|)/(1 +/- |beta|)) because gamma^2(1 -/+ |beta|)^2 = (1 -/+ |beta|)/(1 +/- |beta|); the wavelength ratios are the reciprocals. The receding/approaching identification uses the fixed protocol: the source is at rest in x and the wave propagates from it, so s = beta_hat means the x'-rest observer moves away from the source and s = -beta_hat means it moves toward it. (iv) beta . s = 0 gives omega' = gamma omega from (i); beta . s = |beta|^2 gives omega' = gamma(1 - |beta|^2) omega = omega/gamma, and the equivalence with s' . beta_hat = 0 is the displayed identity; the two cases are distinct because a unit s with beta . s = 0 is not a unit s with beta . s = |beta|^2 when |beta| > 0. The existence of both configurations for every |beta| < 1 is exhibited by the examples on the companion page. (v) Divide the axis formula s'_1 = (s_1 - beta)/(1 - beta s_1) by beta = |beta| for the component along beta_hat (equivalently use s' . beta_hat = (beta . s - |beta|^2)/(|beta|(1 - beta . s)) and divide numerator and denominator by |beta|) to get cos theta_x' = (cos theta_x - |beta|)/(1 - |beta| cos theta_x); the map is the restriction of the Mobius map with positive derivative (1 - |beta|^2)/(1 - |beta| u)^2 > 0 on [-1,1] and fixes the endpoints +1, -1. (vi) The scope clause records the hypotheses and the exclusions; no step uses a source or detector model, and no choice principle is used. The postulate post-sr-ideal-plane-wave-model supplies the physical interpretation of theta, k and the reading rule, and the two other postulates supply the model's light and covariance clauses; the deduction is conditional on all of them.

full_statement_strategy_actually_read.title: Adopted ideal plane-wave and frequency-reading model
full_statement_strategy_actually_read.statement: Adopt as physical assumptions of this framework, extending post-sr-ideal-clocks-and-light (ideal vacuum light rays are exactly the future null straight lines, with coordinate speed c in every inertial chart) and post-sr-inertial-covariance (the affine Minkowski model, with the model's equations covariant under proper orthochronous affine Lorentz maps): (i) Ideal plane wave. An ideal monochromatic light wave in vacuum is modeled, in any inertial chart, by a dimensionless affine phase theta with future null wave covector k (def-sr-affine-phase-and-wave-covector, lem-sr-null-covector-frame-data): the level sets of theta are the wave fronts, every line p + R k^sharp has constant phase, and the rays of this ideal wave are the future null straight lines p + R_{>=0} k^sharp, consistently with the general ideal-light clause that the ideal vacuum light rays are exactly the future null straight lines. The model is one ideal plane wave: constant wave covector, no medium, no dispersion, no absorption, no modulation or envelope, no boundary or source model, no intensity or polarization model. (ii) Frequency reading. An ideal observer of the model with four-velocity U_o = c n (n future unit timelike) that receives this wave reads the angular frequency omega_n := -c k(n) = -k(U_o) and the linear frequency omega_n/(2 pi) of def-sr-null-wave-covector-and-observer-frequency, i.e. minus the rate of change of the phase with respect to the observer's own proper time with the sign convention that this number is positive (lem-sr-phase-rate-along-worldline, lem-sr-future-causal-pairing-negative). The reading is attached to the observer's worldline at the event of reception. (iii) Frequency comparisons. Comparing the frequency of one wave between two ideal observers or between two inertial descriptions means comparing omega_n at specified reception events, or the frame data (omega,s) of the same phase function in specified inertial charts; this postulate asserts no Doppler or aberration formula, and comparing events requires propagating the phase along the specified observer worldlines. (iv) Scope and exclusions. These are adopted idealizations, not deductions from experiment and not claims about nature. No quantum photon model and no identification of energy with hbar omega is made (excluded by the conventions of def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions); no claim is made that real light, real clocks, real receivers or real sources are exactly described; dispersive, absorbing, nonlinear or modulated media, finite line width, intensity, polarization, source and detector physics, gravitation, quantum effects and accelerated-observer reception are outside the model. Empirical tests of the model belong to the framework's experimental work and are not asserted here.
full_statement_strategy_actually_read.strategy: A postulate, not a theorem: it fixes the physical interpretation of the mathematical phase functions and of the observer-frequency number, and it fixes the ideal wave and receiver regime. Obligations: (i) the phase functions with future null wave covectors and their level sets are mathematical objects supplied by def-sr-affine-phase-and-wave-covector and lem-sr-null-covector-frame-data; the identification of the level sets with wave fronts and of the future null lines along k^sharp with this wave's rays is adopted, extending the ideal-light clause of post-sr-ideal-clocks-and-light; for a single plane wave every future null straight line of constant phase is exactly a line p + R_{>=0} k^sharp, so the adoption introduces no competing ray system. (ii) The reading rule is an identification of a physical clock reading of a periodic process with the mathematical number -k(U_o); the mathematical positivity and the proper-time derivative are lem-sr-phase-rate-along-worldline and lem-sr-future-causal-pairing-negative, while the identification itself is adopted. (iii) The postulate is deliberately silent about Doppler and aberration formulas, so it cannot be used to infer them; the comparison protocol is fixed so that downstream theorems state exactly which frequencies at which events they compare. (iv) The exclusions are part of the adopted content and must travel with every conclusion. No proof is manufactured; no choice principle is used.

full_statement_strategy_actually_read.title: Null wave covectors, frame frequency data and the observer frequency of an ideal plane wave
full_statement_strategy_actually_read.statement: Adopt the SI coordinate and unit conventions of def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions: in every inertial chart x^0 = c t with c > 0 in metres per second and spatial coordinates in metres, so c is the model's conversion constant. Let k be a future null wave covector and theta its affine phase (def-sr-affine-phase-and-wave-covector). (a) Frame data as wave data. In the inertial chart of a frame let (varpi,s) be the frame data of lem-sr-null-covector-frame-data, so varpi = -k(e_0) > 0 and |s| = 1. Define the angular frequency omega := c varpi (unit s^-1), the linear frequency nu := omega/(2 pi) (unit s^-1, hertz), the wave vector kappa := (omega/c) s (unit m^-1; |kappa| = omega/c), the wavelength lambda := 2 pi/|kappa| = 2 pi c/omega = c/nu (unit m), and the propagation direction s (dimensionless). In these conventions the phase is theta(p) = -omega t + kappa . x_vec(p) + const with t := x^0(p)/c the coordinate time in seconds, so the components of k in the chart are k_a = (-omega/c, (omega/c)s_1, (omega/c)s_2, (omega/c)s_3). (b) Observer frequency. For an ideal observer whose four-velocity is U_o = c n with n in V future unit timelike (eta(n,n) = -1; def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration, thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition) define the observer angular frequency of the wave as omega_n := -c k(n) = -k(U_o) in s^-1, and the observer linear frequency as omega_n/(2 pi); by lem-sr-phase-rate-along-worldline this is minus the rate of change of the phase with respect to the observer's own proper time, and the sign convention makes it positive. (c) Well-definedness. varpi = -k(e_0) > 0 and |s| = 1 in every inertial frame (frame-data lemma), hence omega > 0 and lambda > 0 are well defined and independent of the choices made in their computation; omega_n > 0 for every future unit timelike n and every future null wave covector (lem-sr-future-causal-pairing-negative), so every ideal observer reads a positive angular frequency; omega_n depends only on k and the observer vector n. (d) This item fixes definitions, units and sign conventions only. It does not assert that any physical light is described by such a phase; that identification is adopted in post-sr-ideal-plane-wave-model. It contains no quantum identification of energy with hbar omega, no amplitude or intensity content, no medium or dispersion model, no source or detector model and no measurement or empirical claim.
full_statement_strategy_actually_read.strategy: Formulation obligations, not a proof of a physical claim. (a) The definitions are functions of k and the frame; well-definedness of varpi and s is lem-sr-null-covector-frame-data and the SI conversion is def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions, so the physical names attached to the mathematical numbers are a convention fixed here. The relation theta(p) = -omega t + kappa . x_vec(p) + const is the substitution x^0 = c t in k_a x^a. (b) n = U_o/c is future unit timelike by thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition(a); omega_n = -c k(n) = -k(U_o) by linearity; positivity and the proper-time-derivative reading are lem-sr-future-causal-pairing-negative and lem-sr-phase-rate-along-worldline with the sign convention explicitly chosen here. (c) Positivity and frame-independence are the quoted lemmas. (d) The scope clause records that the physical interpretation (light is described by an ideal plane wave, and the number defined here is the frequency an ideal observer reads) is adopted only in post-sr-ideal-plane-wave-model; the definition item must not be presented as implying it. No proof of a physical claim is manufactured; no choice principle is used.

full_statement_strategy_actually_read.statement:
Adopt the SI conventions of [[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]], the ideal-clock and ideal-light assumptions of [[post-sr-ideal-clocks-and-light]], the ideal plane-wave and frequency-reading model of [[post-sr-ideal-plane-wave-model]], the operational radar protocol of [[def-sr-operational-radar-protocol]], the massive-particle measurement identification of [[post-sr-massive-particle-dynamics]] clause (ii) and the massless-particle measurement identification of [[post-sr-ideal-massless-particle-momentum]] clause (ii). This definition introduces the framework's experimental-interface vocabulary; it selects no experiment, records no value and asserts no comparison.

**(a) Run descriptions.** A *run description* is a finite tuple $D=(d_1,\dots,d_r)$ whose entries are framework objects of the following kinds, each declared with its domain and regularity as specified by the cited item, together with the frame, observer, event or unit convention required for a numerical reading where such a reading is used: a point of the affine Minkowski space $A$ (an event, [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]); a vector of $V$ of declared causal character ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]); a future timelike worldline together with its proper-time function ([[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]], [[def-sr-proper-time]]); a future unit timelike vector or a smooth observer congruence ([[def-sr-chart-tetrad-and-congruence-distinction]]); a future null wave covector with its affine phase ([[def-sr-affine-phase-and-wave-covector]]); a radar time or radar distance assigned by the operational radar protocol ([[def-sr-operational-radar-protocol]]); an observer angular frequency ([[def-sr-null-wave-covector-and-observer-frequency]]); an observer energy, spatial momentum, kinetic energy or invariant mass ([[def-sr-observed-energy-momentum-and-kinetic-energy]]); and a real parameter vector in a declared subset of $\mathbb R^m$ with declared units. A run description is a description of a model configuration; the tuple asserts nothing about any apparatus or about nature.

**(b) Operational model.** An *operational model* is a tuple $M=(S,\Theta,\theta,D,F)$ in which: $S$ is a nonempty set, the *preparation index set*; $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is a nonempty *parameter set* and $\theta:S\to\Theta$ is a surjection, the *parameter map*; $D$ assigns to each $s\in S$ a run description $D(s)$ of (a); and for some integer $d\ge1$ the map $F:\Theta\to\mathbb R^d$ is a *prediction map* for $D$, subject to the declared interpretation $(*)$: for every $s\in S$, each component of $F(\theta(s))$ is a number that the framework's definitions, postulates and proved consequences assign to the description $D(s)$, with every intermediate quantity, frame, event, sign and unit declared. A pair $(M,F)$ is called an operational model for the quantity whose values $F$ computes. Condition $(*)$ is a declared interpretation that reviewers check when the model is used; it is not a consequence of the tuple structure, and no clause of this definition asserts that any apparatus realizes $M$ or that $F(\theta(s))$ is measured.

**(c) Data records.** A *data record* is a tuple $R=(N,z,\varepsilon,a)$ with an integer $N\ge1$; $z=(z_1,\dots,z_N)$ with $z_k\in\mathbb R^d$; $\varepsilon=(\varepsilon_1,\dots,\varepsilon_N)$ with $\varepsilon_k\in[0,\infty)^d$; and $a=(a_1,\dots,a_N)$ a finite tuple of *condition annotations*, each a finite string identifying the declared run condition of the datum and, when the datum is taken from a report, the bibliographic identification of that report. The record declares: for each $k$, the value of the quantity of (b) under the condition annotated by $a_k$ lies in the closed box $\prod_{j=1}^d[z_{k,j}-\varepsilon_{k,j},\,z_{k,j}+\varepsilon_{k,j}]$, in the declared units. Scope-and-queue record for the empirical layer of the flat special-relativity framework, stated in the vocabulary of [[def-sr-experiment-interface-vocabulary]].

(i) No primary report has been read in the construction of this page; this page records no experiment item, no dataset, no measured value, no calibration, no uncertainty value and no statistical analysis.

(ii) The source design declares four *primary-report search destinations* for future experiment items of this framework. Each is named here as a destination, that is, a family of published reports to retrieve and read in full text, and none of them is evidence for any postulate: (a) historical ether and light-propagation experiments (interferometric or resonance tests of the constancy of the coordinate speed of light between inertial charts, and Doppler-shift tests of moving emitters); (b) unstable-particle lifetime measurements (beam or storage-ring measurements of a particle's lifetime at a measured speed compared with its lifetime at rest); (c) accelerator kinematics of charged particles at high Lorentz factor (measurements of momentum, energy or speed relating a particle's measured quantities to its velocity); (d) clock-transport and clock-comparison experiments (aircraft-, satellite- or laboratory-borne atomic clocks comparing the elapsed times of differently moving or differently situated ideal clocks). The secondary narratives consulted for this page mention instances of these families, among them the historical ether-and-Maxwell context (Crowell pp. 13-15), the 1938 Ives-Stilwell Doppler test (Crowell p. 57), storage-ring muon-lifetime measurements (Crowell pp. 28-29), the 1971 Hafele-Keating aircraft atomic-clock comparison (Crowell pp. 15, 26, 28; Tong pp. 24-25) and a 2010 low-speed atomic-clock measurement (Crowell p. 28); those mentions are contextual motivation only and are not documentation of reported measurements here.

Textbook and review narratives are not substitutes for the primary reports.

(iv) The comparison of model predictions with recorded data is a separate promised physics-theorem obligation which the source design declares to require the primary-report and analysis layer (research label M20); that layer is not supplied, so no experiment item is authored and no comparison is stated until actual reports are read.

(v) Qualifications any future comparison must carry: observations test the combined model and apparatus assumptions; finite-sample agreement does not establish a postulate or a model; a p-value would not be the probability that a theory is false and a confidence level would not be a posterior probability; and a finite bounded record does not by itself determine a unique parameter or adjudicate between distinct models.

after.physical_scope: Formulation vocabulary inside the flat special-relativity framework: it names run descriptions, operational models, data records, calibration declarations and uncertainty bounds built from the framework's own objects (events, worldlines, clocks, observers, ideal waves, radar readings, observer energies and frequencies) and its SI conventions. It asserts no measurement, no apparatus behaviour, no realized experiment, no sampling law, no statistical inference and no value of any physical constant; in particular it does not claim that any laboratory realizes an operational model.
after.statement:
Adopt the SI conventions of [[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]], the ideal-clock and ideal-light assumptions of [[post-sr-ideal-clocks-and-light]], the ideal plane-wave and frequency-reading model of [[post-sr-ideal-plane-wave-model]], the operational radar protocol of [[def-sr-operational-radar-protocol]], the massive-particle measurement identification of [[post-sr-massive-particle-dynamics]] clause (ii) and the massless-particle measurement identification of [[post-sr-ideal-massless-particle-momentum]] clause (ii). This definition introduces the framework's experimental-interface vocabulary; it selects no experiment, records no value and asserts no comparison.

**(a) Run descriptions.** A *run description* is a finite tuple $D=(d_1,\dots,d_r)$ whose entries are framework objects of the following kinds, each declared with its domain and regularity as specified by the cited item, together with the frame, observer, event or unit convention required for a numerical reading where such a reading is used: a point of the affine Minkowski space $A$ (an event, [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]); a vector of $V$ of declared causal character ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]); a future timelike worldline together with its proper-time function ([[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]], [[def-sr-proper-time]]); a future unit timelike vector or a smooth observer congruence ([[def-sr-chart-tetrad-and-congruence-distinction]]); a future null wave covector with its affine phase ([[def-sr-affine-phase-and-wave-covector]]); a radar time or radar distance assigned by the operational radar protocol ([[def-sr-operational-radar-protocol]]); an observer angular frequency ([[def-sr-null-wave-covector-and-observer-frequency]]); an observer energy, spatial momentum, kinetic energy or invariant mass ([[def-sr-observed-energy-momentum-and-kinetic-energy]]); and a real parameter vector in a declared subset of $\mathbb R^m$ with declared units. A run description is a description of a model configuration; the tuple asserts nothing about any apparatus or about nature.

**(b) Operational model.** An *operational model* is a tuple $M=(S,\Theta,\theta,D,F)$ in which: $S$ is a nonempty set, the *preparation index set*; $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is a nonempty *parameter set* and $\theta:S\to\Theta$ is a surjection, the *parameter map*; $D$ assigns to each $s\in S$ a run description $D(s)$ of (a); and for some integer $d\ge1$ the map $F:\Theta\to\mathbb R^d$ is a *prediction map* for $D$, subject to the declared interpretation $(*)$: for every $s\in S$, each component of $F(\theta(s))$ is a number that the framework's definitions, postulates and proved consequences assign to the description $D(s)$, with every intermediate quantity, frame, event, sign and unit declared. A pair $(M,F)$ is called an operational model for the quantity whose values $F$ computes. Condition $(*)$ is a declared interpretation that reviewers check when the model is used; it is not a consequence of the tuple structure, and no clause of this definition asserts that any apparatus realizes $M$ or that $F(\theta(s))$ is measured.

**(c) Data records.** A *data record* is a tuple $R=(N,z,\varepsilon,a)$ with an integer $N\ge1$; $z=(z_1,\dots,z_N)$ with $z_k\in\mathbb R^d$; $\varepsilon=(\varepsilon_1,\dots,\varepsilon_N)$ with $\varepsilon_k\in[0,\infty)^d$; and $a=(a_1,\dots,a_N)$ a finite tuple of *condition annotations*, each a finite string identifying the declared run condition of the datum and, when the datum is taken from a report, the bibliographic identification of that report. The record declares: for each $k$, the value of the quantity of (b) under the condition annotated by $a_k$ lies in the closed box $\prod_{j=1}^d[z_{k,j}-\varepsilon_{k,j},\,z_{k,j}+\varepsilon_{k,j}]$, in the declared units. A data record contains no probability space, random variable, distribution, sampling law, independence assumption, likelihood or coverage statement; it declares nothing about how the values $z_k$ were produced and nothing about the correctness of any calibration.

**(d) Calibration declarations.** Let $Z$ be a nonempty set of declared *instrument-output values*. A *calibration declaration* is a tuple $C=(Z,c,\delta,h)$ with $c:Z\to\mathbb R^d$, $\delta:Z\to[0,\infty)^d$ and $h$ a condition annotation; it declares that for every $z\in Z$ obtained under the condition annotated by $h$, the value of the declared quantity lies in the closed box $\prod_j[c_j(z)-\delta_j(z),\,c_j(z)+\delta_j(z)]$ in the declared units. A *calibration record* is a data record of (c) whose declared quantity is the value of the calibration map's output. The declaration asserts no accuracy beyond the bound $\delta$ and no statistical property of $c$ or $\delta$.

**(e) Uncertainty vocabulary.** For a data record of (c), the *declared uncertainty* of the $k$-th datum is the vector $\varepsilon_k$; a *source label* is an element of the finite declared set $\{\text{calibration},\ \text{systematic},\ \text{sampling-variability},\ \text{rounding},\ \text{other}\}$ attached to a bound; and a *total declared bound* for a value computed from finitely many recorded values by a declared finite arithmetic expression is any $B\in[0,\infty)$ for which the declaration states: whenever each recorded value lies in its declared closed box, the computed value lies in $[\hat y-B,\hat y+B]$ for the declared number $\hat y$ (for instance, for a sum of recorded scalars the sum of the recorded bounds is such a bound). Every uncertainty entry is a declared constraint of the form in (c) and (d); no probability law, coverage probability, confidence level, p-value or posterior is defined by this vocabulary.

**(f) Comparison claims are separate.** A claim that a data record $R$ and an operational model $M$ are consistent, or that $R$ supports, refutes or fails to distinguish $M$, is not part of (a)-(e): it requires its own statement, an explicitly declared comparison rule and adequate primary-report and analysis prerequisites. For the current stored-lithium-ion optical Doppler report, that research prerequisite, labelled M20 in the source design, is supplied by `exp-sr-stored-lithium-ion-doppler-time-dilation-2014` and `pthm-sr-specified-model-comparison`. The comparison theorem distinguishes hard-bound records of (c) from separately defined source-reported estimates and standard-uncertainty scales; the latter are not hard bounds or coverage guarantees. It permits comparison with specified alternative prediction hypotheses, which are not thereby operational models of the SR framework and are not asserted to satisfy condition $(*)$ in (b). Other primary-report families remain subject to their own retrieval and analysis obligations. These are nonlogical status pointers to the separate empirical record and comparison claim; no clause of this vocabulary licenses a conclusion about the truth of a postulate or of the framework.

**(g) Well-definedness and scope.** All components of (a)-(e) are finite tuples of sets, maps and real numbers with declared domains and units; the constructions use no choice principle and no measurability, integrability, completeness or differentiability beyond the cited items, and clause (b) evaluates a prediction only at parameter values for which the cited items supply its ingredients. The vocabulary asserts no measurement, no apparatus behaviour, no empirical support or refutation, no value of the constant $c$ or of any other physical parameter, and no statistical inference.
after.strategy: A definition item. Well-definedness: (a) enumerates object kinds each supplied by a cited item with its own domain and regularity, and requires the reading conventions to be declared rather than inferred; (b) is a tuple of a set, a subset of $\mathbb R^m$, two maps and a finite tuple, all of them finite data with declared domains; the map $F$ is evaluated only at the parameter values $\theta(s)$ for which the cited items define its ingredients; (c) and (d) are finite tuples of real vectors, nonnegative bounds and annotation strings, so each closed box $\prod_j[z_j-\varepsilon_j,z_j+\varepsilon_j]$ is a well-defined subset of $\mathbb R^d$ because $\varepsilon_j\ge0$; (e) defines the declared-bound vocabulary by a stated property rather than by an extremal or optimality claim, and (f) states the separateness of comparison claims. Condition $(*)$ of (b) is deliberately an interpretation obligation: the definition names the tuple and its intended reading, and any use of an operational model must check $(*)$ against the specific framework items (for the Doppler instance of this page, [[pthm-sr-null-wave-doppler-and-aberration]] supplies it). No choice principle is used anywhere: all constructions are finite tuples and pointwise evaluations. The scope clauses exclude measurements, apparatus behaviour, calibration correctness and all statistical notions; the reader should note that an operational model is a mathematical structure of the framework and not a claim that any laboratory realizes it.
